- să începeți rutina de culcare între 18:30 și 20:00, cu culcare între 19:00 și 20:30 - astea sunt din programul de pornire al aplicației până când jurnalul ei are mai multe zile, sunt doar estimări, nu un sfat

outcomes.text: Cum curatam corect biberonul si suzeta?
outcomes.caption:
Pentru biberon și suzetă ajuta mult o rutină simplă după fiecare folosire:

- clătește-le repede cu apă rece sau caldă, apoi demontează tot - tetină, inel, capac.
- spală fiecare piesă separat cu apă caldă și detergent de vase, cu o perie curată doar pentru ele, și clătește bine.
- lasă-le la scurs cu gura în jos pe un prosop curat sau un uscător, să se usuce la aer.

Ține peria și buretele doar pentru lucrurile bebelușului și schimbă-le când se tocesc, iar dacă tetinele sunt crăpate sau lipicioase e bine să le înlocuiești.

outcomes.text: what can we do with her during awake time at 3 months?
outcomes.caption:
For awake time with her right now, you can keep it simple and cozy:

- chat, sing and make faces back at her, pausing so she can coo back
- read one short board book together, letting her look and touch the pages
- some floor time on a blanket with a couple of soft toys within reach
- gentle movement - bicycle legs, arms up, slow dance around the room with her
- a short outing for fresh air, in the carrier or stroller, just narrating what you see

Short little bursts with a cuddle or rest in between are plenty - you can follow her lead and stop when she looks away or gets fussy.

outcomes.text: any simple songs or rhymes to sing while changing him?

- "This is the way we change your diaper, change your diaper, change your diaper" - to the tune of Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush
- "Head, shoulders, knees and toes" - with little touches as you name each part
- "Row, row, row your boat" - with a gentle bounce of his legs at the end
- "Twinkle, twinkle, little star" - nice and calming if he is wiggly

You can also just narrate what you are doing in a sing-song voice - "now we lift the legs up, now we wipe, now fresh diaper on" - little ones love that rhythm and your face close to theirs.

outcomes.text: first trip by train with the baby next week, tips for the journey?
outcomes.caption:
First train trip - exciting! For a 20-week-old, the key is easy access to everything you'll need on board.

Think in layers:
- Seats: aim for a window spot with a bit extra space if you can, and keep the carrier or wrap handy for boarding and for naps on you.
- Feeding and changing: pack bottles / nursing cover if you use one, plus an extra change of clothes for the baby and a t-shirt for you, plenty of diapers and wipes in a small bag on top so you don't dig in the station.
- Rhythm: check your log before you leave so you set off after a feed and with time for a nap on the train - the motion helps a lot of babies doze off.
- Play bag: one soft book, one rattle or teether, and your singing voice and peek-a-boo are plenty for this age. A walk up and down the aisle is great entertainment too.

If you two travel together, split roles - one handles baby, one handles bags and tickets. And keep snacks and water for yourselves within reach.

outcomes.text: how can we make bath time calmer and more fun?

For more fun you could try one or two of these:
- sing the same little bath song each time, with gentle splashing to the rhythm
- let the baby kick and pat the water, and copy her sounds back
- bring one simple toy like a cup or a soft cloth for squeezing and chewing
- end with the same cozy steps — towel cuddle, a little massage, pajamas — so she knows what comes next

- one of you takes the first part of the night, say until 2 or 3am, while the other sleeps uninterrupted in another room with earplugs
- then you swap, so the second person gets the second long stretch until morning

It helps to agree the swap time in advance and keep bottles / diapers ready where the on-duty person can reach them without waking the other. You could alternate who gets first pick every few nights, so it stays fair.

A simple plan that works for lots of couples:

* Split the evening: the partner who starts early does bath + bedtime, then heads to sleep early. The other takes over for any late evening wake.
* Prep Monday in advance together: work clothes out, diaper station restocked, bottles / pump parts washed, bag by the door.
* Agree the night shift: for example, early-starter is officially off-duty until a set time like 4 or 5am, so they can sleep without listening out.

outcomes.text: how do we share the housework more fairly now?

A few ideas that help a lot of tired parents:

- List everything for a week — cooking, bottles, laundry, night wake-ups — and then pick owners for each, so nothing is just "whoever notices it"
- Try shifts instead of both being half-awake: for example one of you is on call until 2am, the other after, so you each get one protected stretch
- Trade the invisible jobs too, like planning meals, tracking diapers, calling family back — those count just as much
- Have a quick 5-minute check-in every couple days: what's working, what's too much, what to swap next

What feels most uneven at the moment — the daytime chores, the nights, or the mental planning?

outcomes.text: my in-laws want to visit every day, how do we set kind limits?

It helps to decide together first what feels doable, like 2-3 shorter visits a week with a rest day in between, and then share it as a team with warmth: you love that they want to see the baby, and you need predictable quiet time to keep a rhythm.

A few things that often make it easier:

- Give a clear window, for example "come 4 to 5:30" rather than open-ended afternoons
- Keep one visit-free stretch in the day for naps and just the three of you
- Give them a concrete way to help if they want to come more often, like bringing a meal or holding the baby while you rest, and it's fine to say today is not a good day
- Let your partner be the one to tell them, so it stays easy on both sides
